channel.title: Daily Recap — 🔬 AI Research
channel.description: What happened in 🔬 AI Research, recapped daily from subscribed feeds.

item.title: Import AI 479: Spacewar, low-latency tasks versus LLMs, and Genie 4
item.description:
The latest Import AI newsletter leads with Spacewar — asking what LLMs think about vision models — alongside a look at low-latency tasks versus LLMs and coverage of Genie 4, Google DeepMind's world model.

The through-line is a practical question for builders: where do large language models fit when a task demands real-time responses, and what do the newest world models imply for agents that need to understand and act in visual environments? It's the research frontier where language, vision, and action are converging.

Sources

  • Import AI: Import AI 479: Spacewar; low-latency tasks versus LLMs; Genie 4

item.title: llm 0.37 ships with new models, easier endpoint setup, and a cheaper default
item.description:
Simon Willison released llm 0.37, the latest version of his CLI tool and Python library for working with large language models, collecting about two months of features and fixes. The release adds gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-terra, plus a new command to make configuring additional OpenAI-compatible endpoints easier.

Most notably, the default model — for users who haven't set their own — switches to gpt-6-luna, at half the price of the previous default. For a tool whose whole purpose is making LLMs accessible from the command line, a cheaper, capable default lowers the barrier for everyone experimenting with models.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: llm 0.37

item.title: Building legal agents when you can't see the data
item.description:
Two Latent.Space conversations with Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora, tackle one of the hardest problems in applied AI: building agents for lawyers when the data belongs to the law firms' clients, meaning Legora can't read a single trace of what its agent does.

The discussions cover evals without traces, million-cell tabular document reviews, and cracks in the billable hour as a business model. It's a case study in building serious AI under the strictest data constraints — where you can't look at your own product's output, and have to engineer trust without observation.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: Building AI for Lawyers - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
  • Latent.Space: Building Legal Agents When You Can't See the Data - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora

item.title: The Zvi: Scott Alexander's case against SURA 'seems deeply confused'
item.description:
The Zvi takes on Scott Alexander's argument against SURA — the AI safety debate's latest flashpoint — arguing that it is deeply confused. The core of the rebuttal is blunt: if you are helping build something that might kill everyone, maybe stop doing that.

The exchange matters because it's not just a blog feud; it's the ongoing argument inside the AI safety community about whether, and how, to slow or steer the development of powerful AI systems. When two of the rationalist community's most-read voices disagree this sharply, the fault lines of that debate come into focus.

Sources

  • The Zvi: Scott Alexander’s Against SURA Seems Deeply Confused

item.title: Hugging Face proposes model integration contracts for Transformers
item.description:
Hugging Face published a post on Model Integration Contracts for its Transformers library — a proposal for formalizing how models integrate with the library, so that new architectures plug in cleanly and predictably.

It's infrastructure work, not a headline model release, but it's the kind of plumbing that determines whether the open model ecosystem stays composable as architectures proliferate. For anyone building on Transformers, the contract proposal is worth reading before the next wave of models arrives.

Sources

  • Hugging Face Blog: Transformers Model Integration Contracts

item.title: What the Census Bureau's AI numbers really say about adoption
item.description:
Simon Willison revisited a chart from Apollo Global Management, based on U.S. Census Bureau numbers, that appeared in September 2025 to show a slowdown in corporate AI adoption among large companies. Re-running the numbers, he examines what the data actually says — and how easily an adoption chart can be misread.

The post is a useful reminder that the AI adoption debate runs on statistics that are easy to over-interpret. The Census Bureau's figures are among the few hard numbers in a conversation dominated by vendor claims, and Willison's re-analysis shows why they deserve a closer look before anyone declares the boom over — or unstoppable.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”

item.title: Python 3.15 tip: if in doubt, delete the uv.lock file
item.description:
Simon Willison's rule of thumb after switching to Python 3.15: if you're getting confusing dependency errors, delete the uv.lock file first. Stray lockfiles left behind by uv run commands can pin a dependency version that doesn't yet have a Python 3.15 wheel, producing errors that look far more mysterious than their cause.

It's a small, practical fix — libraries shouldn't ship lockfiles, but stray ones in .gitignore'd project directories still bite. If your 3.15 upgrade is throwing odd resolver errors, the lockfile is the first suspect, not your code.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file

item.title: Kyle Kingsbury: LLMs are eroding trust in documentation and software
item.description:
Quoting Jepsen's Kyle Kingsbury, Simon Willison highlights a deeper problem with LLMs: they erode trust in documentation, in software, and in the organizations that produce them. The signals engineers once relied on as markers of a mature system are now easy to counterfeit, leaving users unsure what to believe.

Kingsbury's challenge to maintainers is twofold: do the work to ensure correct software and accurate documentation, and then find ways to demonstrate that quality to users in an age when polished-looking output is cheap. It's a question the whole field is now forced to answer.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: Quoting Kyle Kingsbury

item.title: Researchers hijack ChatGPT accounts through its HTML preview sandbox
item.description:
Security researchers at Parameter Labs found a complex attack chain against ChatGPT's HTML preview feature (formerly Canvas), which renders interactive custom HTML apps inside a sandboxed iframe. Because that sandbox is the only thing standing between untrusted code and OpenAI's APIs and private user data, the researchers probed it hard — and found a way through, chaining flaws including one in the MathLive JavaScript library OpenAI uses for graph support.

The details matter less than the lesson: as chatbots become app platforms, the sandbox around embedded web content becomes a critical security boundary. OpenAI has presumably patched the chain, but the write-up is a reminder that every new interactive surface in an AI product is a new attack surface too.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts

item.title: Google admits AI Mode is eating Search revenue as AI stocks tumble
item.description:
Google has reportedly acknowledged that its AI Mode is hurting Search revenue, and the market reaction has been brutal: a 15% drop wiping roughly $500 billion in value, described as the worst since the company's 2004 IPO. The piece frames it as a classic innovator's dilemma — Google cannot have its cake and eat it, since answering questions directly in AI Mode means fewer searches, fewer ads clicked, and less revenue from the business that still funds everything else.

The sell-off feeds a growing 'AI bear market' narrative: after years of AI enthusiasm lifting tech stocks, investors are starting to ask when the massive infrastructure spending actually pays off. For Google, the tension is existential — cannibalize Search now, or let rivals do it instead.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: [AINews] Google admits AI Mode hurts Search revenue; -15% $500B drop worst since 2004 IPO. AI Bear Market coming?

item.title: Agents that prompt people: long-horizon AI work in finance
item.description:
Arca's head of AI discusses what it actually takes to run agents on financial work that spans days rather than minutes. The key ingredients: persistent memory so the agent doesn't lose context between sessions, a custom harness built for the firm's specific workflows, and a design where agents prompt people — escalating to humans at the right moments — rather than running fully autonomously.

It's a useful counterpoint to the 'fully autonomous agent' hype. In high-stakes domains like finance, the winning pattern looks less like handing work to an agent and more like building a durable human-agent collaboration, where the agent keeps working over long horizons and knows when to ask.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: Agents Prompt People: Using Agents for Long-Horizon Financial Work

item.title: Someone baked a working NES emulator into a language model's weights
item.description:
Inspired by the earlier qwenputer experiment, Drew Breunig has baked a working emulator for a Nintendo Entertainment System 6502 CPU into the weights of Qwen3.5-4B. The result, dubbed nesformer, can play NES ROMs such as Super Mario Bros — very slowly — running entirely inside the model.

It's a stunt with a serious point: it shows that a language model's weights can implement a general-purpose computer, not just pattern-match text. Breunig shared the prompts used to build the system, opening the door for others to explore what else can be compiled into weights — and what the limits of that trick turn out to be.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: dbreunig/nesformer

item.title: AIE CODE emerges as the coding-agent conference to watch
item.description:
Latent.Space profiles the building of AIE CODE, positioned as the top conference for coding agents, alongside the day's AI news — including Mistral's open-weight release, frontier model monitoring, and recaps of AI discussion across Twitter and Reddit.

The piece reflects how fast coding agents have gone from a niche interest to a field with its own flagship gathering. As agent frameworks multiply and open-weight releases keep pace with frontier labs, a dedicated venue for practitioners to compare notes is arriving at exactly the right moment.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: [AINews] Building AIE CODE: The top Coding Agent Conference

item.title: Anthropic files to go public
item.description:
Anthropic has filed its S-1, the detailed prospectus companies submit ahead of an initial public offering, beginning the formal process of going public. The filing is the week's biggest structural news in AI: it will force the famously secretive lab to disclose its finances, growth, and risks in public for the first time.

The IPO also sharpens the rivalry with OpenAI, which is already responding with moves like doubled usage limits for Pro subscribers. Once Anthropic is a public company, its strategy will be judged quarterly by the market rather than set behind closed doors — a new kind of pressure for a lab that has built its identity around safety and long-term thinking. The S-1 itself will be the document to watch: it should reveal, at last, what the economics of a frontier AI lab actually look like.

Sources

  • The Zvi: AI #192: Anthropic Is Going Public

item.title: Gemini 4 Carbon tops leaderboards, debuts for cyber defenders
item.description:
Google's new frontier model, Gemini 4 Carbon, leads independent evaluations, according to the latest AI news roundup — and its first access is going to a narrow audience: trusted cyber defenders.

The staged rollout is telling. Rather than a general release, Google is putting its strongest model first in the hands of security professionals, where it can be used to find and fix vulnerabilities before it is available more broadly. It's a pattern worth watching: as frontier models grow more capable, labs are increasingly treating initial access as a safety decision, not just a product launch. For the broader market, the leaderboard-topping scores set the bar that rivals will now have to clear.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: [AINews] Gemini 4 Carbon tops leaderboards, launches for cyber defenders

item.title: Can frontier models see past a decoy?
item.description:
A new decoy counting benchmark exposes a gap between seeing and reasoning in frontier models. Elorian's Glimpse tries to bridge it by thinking with images — reasoning visually rather than just describing what it sees.

The distinction matters because vision models are often fluent at describing a scene while failing at tasks that require careful visual counting or resisting a misleading element planted in the image. A benchmark built around decoys tests whether a model actually reasons about what it sees or just pattern-matches to a plausible answer. If approaches like Glimpse close that gap, it would strengthen a weak spot in multimodal models — one that matters anywhere vision is used for real decisions, from robotics to scientific imaging.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: Can Frontier Models See Past a Decoy? Elorian Tests Visual Reasoning

item.title: OpenAI matches Anthropic's API-credits perk for subscribers
item.description:
OpenAI has launched a benefit that mirrors Anthropic's: subscribers on $100, $200, or $500 monthly plans now get the same dollar amount in expiring credits to use with the OpenAI API, applied to one of their API organizations. Anthropic announced an equivalent perk earlier in October for its Max and Team subscribers.

The symmetry is the story. Both labs are now bundling API access into consumer subscriptions, blurring the line between chat products and developer platforms. For subscribers who build with these tools, the credits effectively make experimentation free up to the plan's value — a strong retention hook. For the labs, it's a way to pull hobbyist builders deeper into their ecosystems, betting that today's side project becomes tomorrow's production workload.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: API credits benefit for eligible ChatGPT subscriptions

item.title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous AI models
item.description:
A fascinating account of building Spawn, a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players prompt an in-game agent called Savi to modify the world itself — conjuring a castle, then a dragon, then riding the dragon around the castle. Behind the scenes, the world is run by autonomous 'Fable-class' models doing agentic engineering against frontier models.

Spawn is a live experiment in what happens when world-building becomes conversational: the game is less a fixed product than a substrate that players reshape in real time. That makes it both a compelling demo of agentic systems and a stress test of their reliability, cost, and coherence at scale. If autonomous models can sustain a shared, evolving world that players actually enjoy, the same techniques could reshape how interactive software of all kinds gets built.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models

item.title: Anthropic files its S-1, opening the books ahead of an IPO
item.description:
Anthropic has filed its S-1, the full prospectus that precedes a public offering, and the complete text is now available for scrutiny. The filing gives the first detailed public look inside one of the leading AI labs — its finances, growth, risks, and structure — after years of operating largely behind private funding rounds.

For anyone tracking the AI industry, the S-1 is a landmark document: it turns Anthropic from a much-discussed private company into one whose numbers can be checked. Expect close readings of its revenue, costs, and governance in the days ahead, and expect the other labs' IPO timelines to be judged against it.

Sources

  • The Zvi: Anthropic Files Its S-1

item.title: GitHub Octoverse 2026: agentic engineering triples merged pull requests
item.description:
GitHub's Octoverse 2026 report, announced at GitHub Universe, puts stark numbers on the impact of agentic engineering. Merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month, commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month — most of that increase coming in the second half of the year — and the new repository rate doubled to 30.3 million per month.

The figures suggest coding agents have crossed from experiment to default: software is now being produced at a pace that would have been implausible a year ago. The open question is what that volume means for code quality, review, and maintenance — the parts of engineering that don't scale just because output does.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: GitHub Octoverse 2026

item.title: October 2026 is an inflection point for vibe-coded games
item.description:
Simon Willison argues that October 2026 is a new inflection point for coding agents — this time for vibe-coding computer games. He draws a parallel to November 2025, when Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that made their coding agents reliable daily drivers for software engineers; now, he says, Claude Opus 5.5 in particular shows meaningful improvements for building games.

The examples range from small playable games to more ambitious projects, and the claim is that putting real work in now produces something genuinely playable. If the November 2025 inflection reshaped professional coding, this one could do the same for hobbyist and indie game development — lowering the bar from "can code" to "can describe a game."

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: The October inflection point for vibe game development

item.title: Nvidia's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2: promptable, adaptable multilingual transcription
item.description:
Nvidia's new Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe pairs an open, promptable transcription model with Granary v2, a large speech dataset built for adapting it. The pitch is transcription you can steer with text prompts and fine-tune for your own data, rather than a fixed black-box API.

For researchers and builders, the interesting part is the combination: an open model plus the corpus to adapt it. Multilingual, prompt-driven speech recognition has mostly lived behind proprietary services; an open stack with adaptation tooling makes it something teams can own, evaluate, and improve themselves.

Sources

  • Hugging Face Blog: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2: Intelligent Multilingual Transcription You Can Prompt and Adapt

item.title: Model performance is multidimensional — but size still explains most of it
item.description:
Quoting Ted Sanders, Simon Willison highlights a useful tension in how we judge language models: performance is deeply multidimensional, with no guarantee that the model best at math is also best at jokes. Yet much of the variation in performance is explained by a single variable — model size.

Bigger models, in general, are more performant and reliable, cost more per token, and have better recall of esoteric facts. The takeaway is a healthy skepticism toward single-number leaderboards: rankings hide real trade-offs, but the scaling story underneath them remains stubbornly simple.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: Quoting Ted Sanders

item.title: Why agents love Supabase: the backend for the agentic era
item.description:
Latent.Space talks with Supabase's Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson about building the backend for AI agents. As agents move from demos to software that acts on its own, they need databases, auth, storage, and realtime infrastructure that works with autonomous, high-volume access patterns.

Supabase's appeal to agent builders is that it packages those pieces into one platform agents can drive directly. The conversation is a window into the infrastructure layer forming underneath agentic software — less glamorous than the models, but the part that determines whether agents can actually do useful work in production.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: Why Agents Love Supabase

item.title: Anthropic files its IPO prospectus — and the AI world digs into the S-1
item.description:
Anthropic has filed its S-1 prospectus, the formal step toward a public listing, and the AI community spent the day poring over the filing and its implications. The document lays out Anthropic's business in unprecedented detail, giving the public its first full look at the finances of one of the two leading AI labs.

Note: some early commentary circulating alongside the filing carried eye-catching figures that have not been independently corroborated. What is confirmed is the filing itself — the prospectus, the numbers inside it, and the reactions it is drawing from investors and rivals.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: [AINews] Anthropic files its S-1

item.title: How Anthropic ships Claude: separating the model's brain from the agent's hands
item.description:
Anthropic engineers Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang joined Latent Space to explain the engineering behind the Claude Platform, including the launch of Opus 5.5. The central idea is a separation of concerns: the model's "brain" does the reasoning, while the agent's "hands" — the tools, APIs, and scaffolding around it — handle acting in the world.

That split is what lets Anthropic scale managed agents reliably, from API design to deployment. For anyone building on top of frontier models, the episode is a useful look at how the leading labs think about turning a model into a product that can be trusted with real tasks.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: How Anthropic ships Claude with Claude: Separating the Brain from the Hands
  • Latent.Space: How Anthropic ships the #1 LLM in the World safely: Separating the Brain from the Hands

item.title: Liquid AI's LFM3: building specialized multimodal models
item.description:
Liquid AI published a guide to building specialized multimodal models with LFM3, its latest model family. The post walks through how to take a general-purpose multimodal foundation and shape it for a specific use case rather than settling for an off-the-shelf model.

The piece fits a broader shift in applied AI: as base models become commodities, the edge increasingly comes from specialization. LFM3 is positioned as a practical route to that — smaller, targeted models tuned for a particular job instead of one giant model for everything.

Sources

  • Hugging Face Blog: Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

item.title: Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel?
item.description:
A new benchmark from AllenAI asks an uncomfortable question: can large language models reliably judge whether a research idea is actually new? The work tests LLMs on novelty assessment — a task that matters as AI tools increasingly help researchers brainstorm, review papers, and triage ideas.

If models are poor judges of novelty, AI-assisted research risks flooding the field with ideas that look fresh but are not. If they are good, they could become a powerful filter for scientists. The benchmark gives the community a way to measure that capability rather than assume it.

Sources

  • Hugging Face Blog: Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel?

item.title: Coding from the Himalayas with a fully offline AI agent
item.description:
A Latent Space post shows how to set up and run an offline coding agent using OpenCode, Ollama, and Qwen — no cloud connection required. The setup pairs an open agent harness with locally run models, proving that capable AI-assisted coding does not have to depend on an API.

The practical payoff is real: offline agents work on planes, in remote locations, and in secure environments where code cannot leave the machine. As open-weight models keep improving, the gap between local and cloud coding assistance keeps narrowing, and this is a concrete recipe for closing it.

Sources

  • Latent.Space: Coding From the Himalayas With an Offline AI Agent

item.title: A Game Boy Color emulator, running on a conference badge
item.description:
At GitHub Universe this week, Simon Willison found that this year's conference badge is once again a full-blown color-screen computer — and fellow attendee Steve Francia, working with Gemini, got a full NES emulator running on it, then went further with emulators for both the Game Boy and Game Boy Color. With a ROM in hand, you can play The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening on your badge.

It is a delightful bit of conference hacking, and a neat illustration of how far commodity hardware and AI-assisted coding have come: a throwaway badge now has the compute to emulate a classic console, and building the emulator took an afternoon with an AI pair programmer.

Sources

  • Simon Willison's Weblog: Game Boy Color on My Conference Badge
